title: DC-024: the worktree cleanup asked a ledger whether anyone was there
summary:
This session moved into its own worktree, which repo guidance required from the start and it did not
do. Every commit before this one was written directly in the primary checkout — recorded here rather
than quietly corrected, because the register exists for the agent's own defects too.

Cleaning up afterwards produced a worse finding. coord worktree cleanup --remove deleted
C:/Projects/ai-de-facelift reporting "clean, merged, unheld" — and a LIVE session recreated the tree
within the minute and wrote a marker reading "facelift worktree in use". Nothing was lost: the
cleanliness checks were all correct, the tree had no uncommitted work and no unique commits. The
LIVENESS check was the wrong one. It read live_keys — a registration ledger — and that session had
never run coord session start. A ledger says who signed in; it never says nobody is there.

Registered as DC-024 and controlled: worktree_safety now ends with a filesystem condition. A tree
whose files were modified within the last hour is HELD whatever the ledger says. The scan skips build
output, is capped at 4,000 files, and treats hitting the cap as in-use rather than as an answer,
because a partial scan cannot prove absence. The reason string carries the age, so "idle" is a
measurement someone can disagree with rather than a verdict.

Observed failing in both directions on a scratch tree: clean, merged and unregistered it reported
KEEP - touched recently - last modified 0 minute(s) ago; with its files backdated two hours it became
WOULD - clean, merged, unheld, idle - last modified 120 minute(s) ago. A safety rule that never
permits anything is not a safety rule.

title: Panes rendered and read; a second repository finds absence rendered as coverage
summary:
The panes are now rendered and read, and a second repository was measured.

PaneRenderTests walks the visual tree of the Joins and Contexts panes and asserts on CONTENT, never
on a control count — "has four children" passes for four empty labels. In-process on an STA thread
rather than as another out-of-process probe: the canvas needs a real foreground window because it
drives a browser through SendInput, and these panes build their own children. The last case is the
rule both must keep: no evidence pane, in any of its six states, may render no readable text.
Observed failing by making one pane silent.

A crossing dominated by one object now says which one. Found by eye once — 57 of 72 edges were
AppDbContext — and a signal a person has to notice is a signal that gets noticed once. Majority of
the listed members, computed over what was actually examined rather than extrapolated to the full
weight, with the undisclosed count still beside it. Three tests including the boundary: exactly half
is not domination.

BioHacker was measured as a second repository, deliberately a different shape — 25 scopes, 26 Bicep
resources, no Entity Framework. Zero joins is the correct answer there and the pane says so. But it
has no context map, and the pane reported "0 uncovered" and "Every declared symbol belongs to a
context" — the sentence a fully-mapped codebase produces. The arithmetic was right, which is why a
cleverer count could not have fixed it. ContextMapView carries IsDeclared now and says plainly that
nothing has been claimed about the code yet. One repository could not have found this: TheTerrace has
a map, so every path that runs when there is none had never been exercised.

And TheTerrace's Platform split is applied on a branch in its own worktree — docs/platform-context,
committed locally and NOT pushed, because that repository is the user's to publish.

title: A written contract between the core and design sessions
summary:
Two sessions now work this repository at once — core capabilities here, styling and design surfaces
in the other tree. docs/collaboration/session-contracts.md is the proposal, written down because
"we'll coordinate" is not a coordination mechanism and the first thing two sessions lose is not code
but agreement about what each thought was true.

The seam is one sentence: Core produces view models, Design renders them. A view model is a record
with no behaviour and no WPF types, carrying what the user needs to know INCLUDING what could not be
established — a projection that hides a gap forces the surface to invent one. Neither side reaches
across: Core does not choose colour or control, Design does not compute a number, because a number
computed in a surface is a second definition of a quantity that already has one.

File ownership is listed rather than described, with the shared files and the rule each carries.
Derived files — docs-index.js, audit-data.js — are called out because a hand-merged generated file is
a conflict resolved into a lie.

Section 6 is deliberate: what this does NOT settle. Fast-forward versus pull request, whether view
models should carry presentation hints, and where visual regression evidence lives are joint
decisions, and writing one session's preference down as settled is how a proposal becomes a fait
accompli. Status is proposed, not accepted.

Three requests to Design are recorded in 4a rather than made in conversation, each additive and
already on main.

title: One extractor composition, and a bounded read that says what it missed
summary:
Two core defects, both about a boundary telling the truth about itself.

**The running app could not see what the spike could.** The daemon composed only the C# extractor and
the fixture adapter, so infrastructure and schema were invisible to the product while a spike
composed all four and reported joins the app had no way to show — two answers to "what does this tool
read", depending which door you came in. WorkspaceExtractors.Default() is now the single composition,
used by the daemon and the spike, with named arguments.

That matters because the hand-written form is easy to get wrong SILENTLY: the spike once passed its
extractors positionally, which put BicepExtractor in the fallback slot and routed every bicep scope
to the schema extractor. Both failed and the write-up concluded the repository had no Bicep. It has
two templates and 24 resource declarations. CompositeExtractor.RouteFor now exposes the routing
decision so a test can read it, and the test was observed failing on that exact mis-ordering:
expected "bicep", actual "schema".

**Every number both panes show was computed from a bounded read that never said so.** The shell
searches with a 20,000 cap, describes 4,000 of the matches, and takes 60 neighbours from each. On the
repositories measured so far all three are slack — and nothing in the output would change if they
were not. The counts would simply be smaller and still be presented as facts. EvidenceRead carries
what the read did not see; the shell announces it once per distinct sentence, and reports BOTH causes
separately because "bigger than the search cap" and "these nodes are unusually connected" have
opposite fixes. A node returning exactly the limit counts as truncated, because the read cannot tell
the difference and guessing in the flattering direction is how a cap becomes a quieter wrong number.

title: Domain experts + facelift/knowledge/UML-ERM specs and mockups
prompt: domain experts + specify + ui-design chain
summary: Roster 26; flat->soft-islands; node-introspection router; derived read-only UML/ERM.
rationale: Subject-matter judgment + three grounded surfaces.

title: The panes were reading 50 nodes; the search now has its own ceiling
summary:
Two defects the panes had been living with, both about a boundary lying about how much it saw.

**The panes were computing from at most 50 nodes.** ProjectionService.Find borrowed
MaxNeighborsCeiling, which is 50. The workbench asked for 20,000 matches to build the context and
join panes and received 50 — so crossing counts, join counts and coverage were computed from roughly
three percent of a real workspace and presented as the answer, while the spike read the store
directly and showed the whole picture. The two disagreed for days and nothing said so. A search
returns identity columns only, so its payload per row is small and its ceiling can be large;
MaxSearchResultsCeiling is now its own constant at 20,000. On TheTerrace the panes went from 50 nodes
to 2,164.

**And the read reported a total it had made up.** ReadAssertions counted the rows in front of it and
called that the number of matching nodes, while ResultBounds.OmittedNodes had been carrying the true
remainder all along. The shell reads the bounds now. The neighbour limit was also wrong in the other
direction — the shell asked for 60 against a ceiling of 50, so the truncation check compared against
a limit that could never be reached: a control that could not fire, guarding a cap that was already
biting. It reads the service's own constant now, and on TheTerrace it fires for real on 26 nodes.

Also proven across the pipe: the daemon returns infrastructure evidence, asserted against the
provenance extractor id rather than a predicate name. That test first failed against a STALE Release
daemon, because LocateDaemon preferred Release if the folder existed rather than following the
configuration the tests were built in — DC-023 in the harness, fixed.

title: Incremental re-index, and the restart that could never index twice
summary:
Incremental re-index, and two defects it uncovered on the way.

Every index re-extracted every scope: 4.3 seconds on TheTerrace, 2.8 on another repository, paid in
full whether one file changed or none. ScopeFingerprints digests each scope's input files by path,
size and modification time, plus an extractor generation so upgrading the product invalidates
everything rather than leaving a graph built by two extractor versions with nothing saying which.
TheTerrace re-indexes in 0.1s now, ten scopes reused.

The reuse is counted separately from the indexing. "7 of 7 indexed" would be a true sentence about a
run that read nothing, and the question after a surprising graph is always whether it actually
looked. It fails towards re-extraction: an unreadable directory, a missing sidecar or a scope whose
committed evidence has gone all produce a re-read, because the cost of an unnecessary extraction is
seconds and the cost of a skipped one is a graph describing code that no longer exists.

Testing it across a reopen found something unrelated and worse: THE SECOND INDEX OF ANY WORKSPACE
AFTER A RESTART FAILED. The generation counter lives in memory and started at zero on every open
while the store did not, so it re-used generation 1 and violated the desired-generation primary key.
The daemon opens the store fresh every time it starts. Nothing had ever indexed twice across a
reopen, so nothing had ever noticed. Seeded from the store now.

And re-extracting a revision the store already holds surfaced as a raw SQLite UNIQUE-constraint
exception from the middle of a run. The first fix silenced the natural key with INSERT OR IGNORE —
which broke an existing test asserting that key rejects duplicates, and rightly so: that control is
deliberate. The caller is idempotent instead. Re-extracting a revision already committed returns
without writing, the store stays strict, and "index again" answers the user's real question, which
is whether the graph is current for this revision.

title: DC-013 prevented: ids allocated from a lock-guarded counter every worktree shares
summary:
DC-013 is prevented now rather than detected. Three occurrences, the last between two AGENTS rather
than two trees of one — which broke the previous control, because "run log-writing scripts in the
tree where the work is" is advice that cannot reach a session that is not yours.

Every worktree of a repository shares ONE git common directory. A counter placed there is visible to
all of them, and an exclusive-create lock makes the read-modify-write atomic. The file's own highest
id remains the floor, so a counter that is missing, stale or from a fresh clone can only ever be
caught up to reality, never fall behind it.

Sixteen concurrent allocations issued from two different worktrees of this repository returned
sixteen distinct ids. The previous allocator returns the same one to all sixteen. Gaps are expected
and harmless: an id is an identifier, not a count, and the gate checks uniqueness rather than
contiguity. Promoted to controlled, with the honest residual — two separate CLONES do not share a
git directory and would still collide, and a stale lock falls back to the old behaviour by design.

Two more things the fingerprint work needed. The scope SET is part of a workspace's shape and changes
without any individual scope changing, so a departed scope is now reconciled out of the sidecar and
recorded as a health incident rather than reused forever while its evidence describes code that no
longer exists. And a single-file scope is fingerprinted by its own file: treating a Bicep template as
its containing directory made two templates in one infra/ folder share a basis, so deleting either
invalidated both.

title: Force is reachable, and a fourth repository finds absence rendered as emptiness
summary:
Two escape hatches and a fourth repository.

**Force is reachable.** It existed as an API parameter with nothing able to reach it. Ctrl+K, Shift+I
re-reads every scope ignoring the cache, threaded through the wire contract additively — a client
built before the field still decodes and still means "use the cache", which is the safe reading of an
absent flag. The command announces that it is ignoring the cache, because the only reason to run it
is that the user does not trust the fast answer and a command that looks identical gives them no way
to tell which they got. IndexSummary reports reuse in words for the same reason: "Indexed 0 of 7"
with nothing else reads as a failure.

Adding a command required one line in a Design-owned file, because the conformance test makes adding
a command and placing it in a menu one atomic change. Written down rather than done quietly: the
command-to-menu mapping is now recorded as Core-owned DATA inside a Design-owned file, with a
proposal to move it onto the catalog entry so the seam stops crossing there.

**A fourth repository, chosen for what it lacks.** 63 Python files, 40 TypeScript, no C#, no Bicep,
no migrations. It produced zero scopes, zero assertions and an EMPTY DISCLOSURE LIST —
indistinguishable from an empty directory, with the mechanism whose entire job is to say what was not
read saying nothing. Third repository in a row to find the same shape: a missing context map read as
perfect coverage, a bounded search read as the whole workspace, unreadable source read as no source.
Each time the arithmetic was right and the claim was false.

UnanalysedLanguages names what is present and unread, with counts, because "some Python" and "10,760
Python files" are different statements about how much of a repository the graph is silent on.
Vendored directories are excluded and a C#-only workspace discloses nothing, because a disclosure
that fires everywhere is noise.

And the caps fix is now checkable on every run: 122 of 124 join edges agree between the pane read and
the store, the two missing are cut by the neighbour cap, and the shortfall line reports them.

title: The panes read the store exactly: a paged bulk evidence query
summary:
The panes now see exactly what the store holds — 12,100 of 12,100 assertions, 124 of 124 join edges,
zero divergence. They were rebuilding that set node by node through Describe, which bounds neighbours
at 50 and lost two edges doing it, and which asks the store for a graph walk when what is wanted is a
table scan.

EvidenceAsync is the question they were actually asking: one page of every current assertion, paged
because it crosses a pipe and an unbounded response would breach the result-byte cap. The cursor is
the last row's (subject, predicate, object) — the same tuple the ORDER BY uses, so a page boundary
cannot skip or repeat a row; an id-based cursor would order by something the query does not, which is
how paging quietly loses records. A malformed cursor restarts rather than throwing, because it is
opaque and a caller was never meant to construct one.

Pinned with a page size of ONE, so every boundary in the set is exercised: the union of the pages
equals the whole set, nothing repeated. A comfortable page size would test that the query runs, not
that the cursor is right.

Two more things landed with it. A departed scope's evidence is now retired by committing an EMPTY
snapshot at a higher generation — superseded, never deleted, because the store is append-only and
destroying the rows would destroy the record of what the graph once said. Removing a project used to
leave its symbols and crossings in every projection indefinitely. And every catalog command now
declares its menu, so the builder can derive its grouping and Core stops needing to edit a
design-owned file to add a command at all.

title: DC-025 absence rendered as success, and DC-026 a merge that de-duplicates on the disputed key
summary:
Two defect classes registered, one of them mine.

DC-025, absence rendered as success. A projection computes over a set that is empty BECAUSE NOTHING
WAS COLLECTED, the arithmetic is correct, and the surface renders that zero with the vocabulary of
completeness. Four instances now, all found by pointing the panes at real repositories and none by a
test: a missing context map read as perfect coverage; a search bounded at fifty read as the whole
workspace; unreadable source read as no source; and now a file that does not parse. Roslyn does not
throw on broken source — it returns a tree with error nodes — so extraction succeeds and simply finds
less, which is indistinguishable from a smaller file. That is the state a developer is in most often,
and it disclosed nothing. Fixed with source-did-not-parse, which names the files and their count
while still contributing what did parse.

Worth recording honestly: the fourth instance was nearly reported from an experiment that had not
run. The script meant to corrupt a file silently did nothing, and the assertion-count difference I
was about to attribute to a syntax error had another cause entirely. It became a finding only after
the broken file was verified to exist.

DC-026 is mine. Resolving an append-only merge conflict by unioning KEYED BY ID, with setdefault,
silently dropped a design-session entry — the gate stayed green throughout, because uniqueness was
satisfied precisely by the removal. The defect is not the collision; it is de-duplicating on the
field that is in dispute. tools/merge-append-only-log.py unions by content so nothing can be dropped,
re-issues a contested id from the shared counter, and prints the count in, the count out, and every
re-issue — a merge that resolves silently is indistinguishable from one that lost something.

title: A corpus of workspaces defined by what they lack, and a gate that notices a shrinking log
summary:
DC-025 has a control instead of a habit, and the gate that missed DC-026 now looks for the loss.

LackingWorkspaceTests is a corpus of workspaces defined by what they LACK: empty, only-Python, source
that will not parse, no context map, a read that was bounded, and a scope whose extraction failed so
the graph shows an older revision. Every case asserts a SENTENCE, never a count, because the counts
were always right — that is what made the class survive four times. Fixtures always have the thing:
they are written by the person building the feature, so they contain a context map, compile, and are
in the language the extractor reads. This corpus is the deliberate opposite. Its last case is the
generalisation itself — a workspace missing something must never produce a result that is silent
about it — so adding a new kind of absence is how the next instance gets caught before a real
repository finds it.

verify-audit-log.py now compares each log against HEAD and fails when an id present in the committed
version has disappeared. It only counted duplicates before, which is exactly why it stayed green
while my merge removed an entry: uniqueness was satisfied PRECISELY BY the removal. Observed failing
on a log with its last entry deleted. The residual is honest — it sees losses against HEAD, so a loss
introduced and committed in one step is still invisible.

And the paged evidence read is proven across the daemon, at a page size of one so the cursor is
exercised at every boundary rather than the test proving only that a single response deserialises.
The last three cross-boundary defects were all "right in process, wrong through the pipe".

title: Stale scopes are stated, not retracted; and the read scales where extraction does not
summary:
A step changed on inspection, and a measurement taken rather than guessed.

The listed step was "retract on scope failure, not just departure". Opening the code first showed
that keeping the last good snapshot on failure is a DELIBERATE decision, recorded in
RefreshScopeAsync: blanking the graph on a build error would be worse. Retracting would have
contradicted that rather than built on it. The real gap was that what renders is then OLD and nothing
said so — a stale scope drew exactly like a current one, and only the incident sidecar knew. So the
failure now discloses stale-scope with the revision still being shown, and the snapshot keeps
rendering.

Scale, measured on a SYNTHETIC workspace and labelled as such because nothing available here is much
larger than TheTerrace: 20 projects, 2,400 types, 21,066 assertions.

  first index                13.5s  (about 0.68s per project of 120 types, roughly linear)
  re-index, nothing changed   0.1s  (20 scopes reused)
  paged read of everything   185ms  (11 pages, exact agreement with the store)
  shortfall                  none   (no cap bit at 21,066 assertions)

The read is not the problem at this size; extraction is. 185ms to page 21,066 assertions against
13.5s to produce them says the next scale work belongs in the extractor rather than the query path —
and the fingerprint cache already means that 13.5s is paid once rather than per refresh. The honest
limit: this says nothing about deep inheritance, heavy generics or thousands of package references,
because the generator produces none of those. It bounds the shape it tested and no more.

title: INV-0001: a 22,297-character PATH, and cmd.exe drops it
summary:
Reported: "the agent sessions do not have my profile or my environment variables — ghcp and claude
are both installed so they should both work."

The verified cause is not in this product. The machine's PATH is 22,297 characters and cmd.exe
silently drops a variable that large, so every .cmd shim — which is every npm-installed CLI — starts
with an EMPTY PATH and cannot find node, git or itself. claude works because claude.exe is a real
executable with no cmd in the path; ghcp does not exist at all, and the Copilot CLI has an npm .cmd
shim. That asymmetry is the entire symptom.

Necessary and sufficient, both measured: at 22,297 characters a cmd child receives an empty PATH,
reproduced twice including once with no part of AI-DE involved; trimmed to 1,799 characters the same
child receives the full PATH. AI-DE passes the environment correctly — PowerShell started from the
same inherited block reads all 22,297 characters and resolves claude.

Five hypotheses were ruled out with evidence, including one flag removed and re-measured, and the
belief that the profile was at fault — which is where two turns of work went first, because the
symptom is indistinguishable from a launcher bug.

The cause of the 22,297 characters: roughly 190 entries of the shape Temp\biohacker-nuget-<guid>\
dotnet-home\.dotnet\tools, appended to the PERSISTED user PATH by another project's build tooling and
never removed. Each is unique, so there is nothing to de-duplicate.

What was ours is the silence. The terminal opened, looked healthy, and the tools were absent with
nothing saying why. EnvironmentHealth.Inspect now states the size, the limit and the largest repeated
group — because 200 unique paths is a number, not a lead — announced once per shell, never per pane.
It does not edit PATH: a tool that silently rewrites the environment to make itself work has hidden
the problem from the only person who can fix it.

Agents are now hosted in the login shell rather than launched beside it, which delivers the profile
half of the request and makes .ps1 shims resolve. It is recorded honestly as NOT fixing the reported
symptom — a .cmd shim invoked from the hosting shell still starts cmd, which still drops the PATH.
Measured, not assumed.

Registered as DC-027: the environment a parent hands a child is not the one the child receives.

title: The PATH is cleaned, the cmd limit is measured, and extraction is profiled
summary:
The reported symptom is fixed, at its actual cause.

The user PATH went from 21,528 characters and 206 entries to 1,150 and 19. The 187 removed entries
were all of the shape Temp\biohacker-nuget-<guid>\dotnet-home\.dotnet\tools, and every one of them
was ALREADY ABSENT FROM DISK — a directory that does not exist cannot be providing a tool, which is
what made the removal safe rather than a judgement call. The previous value is backed up to
%LOCALAPPDATA%\AiDe\user-path-backup-<timestamp>.txt. Verified after: a .cmd shim in a fresh process
receives the PATH, and both copilot and claude resolve through it.

The cmd limit is now measured rather than quoted. Bisected: cmd carries 8,151 characters and drops
8,152, printing "The input line is too long" and losing the value. The documented figure is 8,191 and
the ~40-character difference is the variable's own name plus block overhead, which is why the message
still says "may be dropped" — not because the number is unmeasured, but because it shifts with the
name.

EnvironmentHealth now measures every variable, not only PATH: any oversized one is dropped by the
same mechanism, and checking only the variable that happened to bite is how a class gets found twice.

And AvailableAgents no longer trusts a filter the environment invalidates. When the environment is
unhealthy the PATH filter is skipped and every agent is offered, because a menu that silently omits
an agent is invisible while a launch that fails is not — and the shell has already said why.

title: 98% of extraction is the read, not the walk
summary:
Extraction profiled, and the answer moves the next optimisation to the other half.

The previous measurement said "the read is not the problem at this size; extraction is" — true and
useless, because it did not say which part of extraction. AIDE_EXTRACTION_TIMING splits each scope
into the READ phase (parse the sources, build the compilation, resolve references) and the WALK phase
(visit symbols, emit assertions):

  read 505-616ms per project, walk 6-15ms once the JIT is warm

Roughly 98% of the cost is the read. The first scope's 260ms walk is JIT rather than work, and a
total without the split would have attributed it to the walk and sent the next optimisation at the
wrong half.

So incremental work belongs in AVOIDING the read — which the fingerprint cache already does per
scope and would do better per file. Making the symbol walk faster would recover about one percent.

Emitted on the normal path as activity tags, with an env var for the console form: a feature is not
done until its behaviour is measurable without a re-run.

title: File I/O is 97% of extraction, not parsing — and a timer that said otherwise
summary:
File-granularity incremental extraction, and a measurement of mine that was wrong twice before it was
right.

The profile said the READ phase is 98% of extraction. Splitting it further produced "parsing is 97%
of the read, so cache the trees" — plausible, confident, and wrong, because the timer wrapped
File.ReadAllText and ParseText together and reported the total as "parse". Timed apart on freshly
written files: read 576-690ms, parse 4-5ms. Disk I/O is ~99% of the read, which makes file I/O
roughly 97% of everything extraction does — the opposite half from the one the bundled timer pointed
at.

It was caught only because a follow-up run produced a 40x speedup with ZERO cache hits, and no
correct model explained that. Appended as an instance to DC-009: an instrument reports what it
measured, so a timer around two operations must be named for both or split.

SyntaxTreeCache was built on the wrong rationale and is right anyway, because a hit skips the whole
factory — the disk read as well as the parse. Keyed by path, length, modification time and the parse
options: hashing the bytes to decide whether to read the bytes is a cache that costs what it saves.
Forced re-index in the same process, with a distinct revision so the store's already-committed
short-circuit could not answer for it: 720 of 720 trees reused, 0ms read, 0ms parse, and the whole
run 1.0s instead of 1.0s+ at 0.6s. This is the case the scope fingerprint cannot cover — one file
edited in a project of a hundred and twenty, where the scope must be re-read and 119 files did not
move.

PATH regrowth is now caught by SHAPE rather than by size. The oversize check only fires once PATH is
past cmd's limit, which is to say after the damage; 187 dead build directories accumulated before
anything noticed. Ten or more entries pointing at directories that do not exist is now a finding,
with the largest group named — so regrowth is caught at twenty entries rather than a hundred and
eighty-seven. A handful of dead entries stays quiet, because this is looking for accumulation rather
than tidiness.

What appends those entries was NOT found: no repository on this machine contains the string, so it
was not a checked-in script. The guard is the durable answer available from here.

title: A second language extractor, and the paging tie it exposed
summary:
A second language, and a paging defect the second language exposed.

PythonExtractor reads modules, top-level classes and functions, and import edges. Six repositories
had disclosed unread Python before it existed; the disclosure was right and it is not a substitute,
because a graph that says "there is Python here and I cannot see it" is honest and still blind.

It reads STRUCTURE, not semantics, and says so on every scope: imports are not resolved, nested
declarations are invisible, dynamic imports are not followed. Declarations are recognised at column
zero only — an indented def is a method, and claiming it as a module-level function would put a
symbol in the graph that no importer can reach. Import edges are INFERRED, because the target is the
module path as written and whether it resolves to anything is not established here; calling that
Verified is precisely the defect DC-022 is about. A simplify: marker records the ceiling and the
upgrade trigger.

Python also came OFF the unanalysed-languages list on the same day, because a closed gap reported as
open is the same defect as an open one hidden.

Measured on the repository that started this: ai-forward produced ZERO assertions and an empty
disclosure list three turns ago. It now produces 2,158 assertions across 5 scopes in 0.2 seconds,
with its remaining gaps named.

And that run exposed a real paging defect: 2,158 in the store, 2,157 through the paged read.
(subject, predicate, object) is NOT unique — two scopes can assert the same triple — so a cursor over
that ordering silently loses exactly the rows that tie, when a page boundary lands on one. Scope is
part of the ordering and the cursor now, and a test builds two identical Python packages to
manufacture the tie deliberately.

The I/O question was measured rather than assumed and is only half answered. Raw reads of 120 files
cost 5ms outside this product and 73ms on first touch from a different process — a 15x first-access
penalty consistent with on-access scanning. Inside the extractor the same volume costs ~500ms, which
is seven times worse again and is NOT explained. Recorded as a gap rather than a claim; the tree
cache removes the cost on re-index whichever explanation turns out to be right.

title: DC-028: the synthetic benchmark was measuring itself
summary:
The extraction profile is explained, and both earlier conclusions were artefacts of the benchmark.

A fresh .NET process reading 120 newly-created files took 493ms (4.11ms/file); a SECOND fresh process
over the same files took 6ms, and the repository's own source reads at 0.19ms/file. So the ~500ms
was a one-time, system-wide, per-file cost on the first read after creation — the signature of
on-access scanning — and it never recurs. It is not extraction's cost at all.

Run against a real repository the profile inverts completely. TheTerrace, 463 files in its main
scope: read 53ms, parse 694ms, walk 1,167ms. The walk is the LARGEST cost on real code and looked
free on the synthetic workload, because the generated types were trivial — no inheritance, no
generics, four fields each.

Two independent flaws in one generator, each inverting a published conclusion. Registered as DC-028:
a synthetic benchmark measures the benchmark unless its workload resembles the real one in the
dimensions that drive cost. The control is that the spike prints the same timings for named real
repositories, so the synthetic figure and the real one appear side by side.

Python imports are resolved within their scope now. An import naming a module the scope contains
points at a file that exists and was read, so the edge is VERIFIED; anything else stays INFERRED with
the name as written, because it may be a package, a module in another scope, or nothing, and
asserting which is the guess DC-022 is about. Relative imports resolve against the importing module's
package, one level per leading dot, and climbing above the root resolves to nothing rather than
throwing. On the real Python repository 82 of 330 imports now resolve, and the disclosure carries the
count of those that do not — a blanket "imports are not resolved" became a closed gap reported as
open the moment resolution landed.

The cursor audit found one more thing and cleared another. ResultBounds.NextCursor is ALWAYS null and
no projection returning it pages — said out loud in the type, because a caller could loop on it and
never leave the first page with nothing failing. And DeriveClaimCurrent folds statuses with Max under
a comment saying the weakest wins: correct only because the enum is ordered strongest-first, so a
reordering would silently invert it into manufacturing confidence. Pinned by a test.

title: The graph surface had never shown a graph: two nodes of 2,813
summary:
The graph surface had never shown a graph.

Reported by the user, comparing TheTerrace in this tool against the same repository in Obsidian: two
nodes versus a full graph. The cause was not extraction — the store held 12,100 assertions across
2,164 nodes — it was that the canvas called FindAsync with a limit of ONE to pick a root and then
drew that root's neighbours. A workspace of two thousand nodes rendered as the alphabetically first
symbol and its single neighbour, correctly, from the day it was written. Four unit tests described
that behaviour approvingly.

GraphProjection answers the question the surface exists for: every node and edge, bounded by a cap
that is reported rather than silent. Attributes fold onto nodes instead of being drawn as edges — a
has_type arrow would put the string "class" in the graph as a thing other things point at — using the
same single definition the search already applies. LoadAsync with no root now means the whole graph;
a root means drill-down. Proven across the daemon as well, because every cross-boundary defect so far
has been right in process and wrong through the pipe.

A second finding sat inside the first. With the graph finally visible, its six most-connected nodes
were string, int, Task<TResult>, DateTimeOffset, IReadOnlyList<T> and Guid — 773 edges to string
alone. A graph whose centre is the BCL is not a picture of anybody's domain, and a cap ordered by raw
degree drops the user's own types to keep framework primitives. Nodes carry IsExternal now (nothing
in the workspace declares them) and declared nodes are kept first. The same repository's centre
became AppDbContext, Fixture, SportMonksProvider, ScheduledRefresh.

Registered as DC-031: a surface asks a narrower question than the one it exists to answer. The
generalisation is one question — what is the cardinality of what this shows, against the cardinality
of what it fetched — and the related tell is a test suite that describes the slice fluently.

TheTerrace now: 28 scopes, 13,530 assertions, 2,813 nodes and 8,602 edges with nothing omitted.

title: TypeScript read, and the symbol walk profiled
summary:
TypeScript is read, and the symbol walk is profiled.

TypeScriptExtractor closes the largest remaining disclosure — typescript-not-analysed (165 files) on
a repository whose C# half was fully mapped. Same bargain as Python: structure, not semantics.
Exported top-level class, interface, type, enum, function and const; import and re-export
specifiers; nothing inside a function or a namespace block. Declaration files (.d.ts) are skipped
because they re-state types defined elsewhere and indexing them would put every symbol in the graph
twice, once with nothing behind it.

Specifiers resolve only when RELATIVE and only to a file this scope contains — extensions optional,
a directory meaning its index file. A bare specifier is a package or a path alias and resolving it
needs configuration this extractor deliberately does not read, so it stays Inferred with the
specifier as written. TypeScript and JavaScript left the unanalysed-languages list the same day.

It is deliberately NOT a shared base with PythonExtractor. They look alike and are not the same:
TypeScript's specifiers carry extensions and index files, its declarations are export-gated rather
than column-zero, and JSX changes what a valid line looks like. A base parameterised by all of that
is more machinery than either extractor contains; a third language that fits the pattern is when the
abstraction is earned.

Indexing TheTerrace with it immediately raised a real store error: two files can share a module name
— app.ts beside a compiled app.js — so the same triple was asserted twice in one scope and the
natural key rejected it, correctly. Identical facts are one fact, so both extractors deduplicate
before returning. Silencing the key would have weakened a control that is doing its job.

And the symbol walk, which the real-repository profile named as the largest cost, is now split:
enumerating the namespace tree is 135ms for 1,026 types, and reading each type's members is 1,074ms
— about 89% of the walk and half the whole scope. The next hypothesis worth testing is
ToDisplayString, called per symbol, but that is a hypothesis and is written down as one rather than
acted on.

title: The join reader recognised one spelling of EF, and module ids collided
summary:
The hypothesis that `ToDisplayString` dominated the symbol walk was **wrong**, and measuring it found
a much larger defect than the one it was looking for.

Splitting the walk by operation: display 46ms across 7,312 calls — **3.9%**. The real costs were
depends-on 613ms (51%) and attributes 403ms (34%). The attribute cost was one call:
`FluentTableMappings` ran `DescendantNodes()` over all 1,026 type declarations, hunting an EF
`ToTable` call. Hoisting it to the compilation with a source-text prefilter cut it to 1ms of
prefilter across 465 files and 217ms of walking the 66 that survived.

Then the 66 files were the finding. Most were EF migration `*.Designer.cs` snapshots — and the three
that were not revealed that the reader **did not work**. It matched `Entity<T>()...ToTable("x")` as a
single expression. TheTerrace, like most EF codebases, writes:

    var terrace = modelBuilder.Entity<Terrace>();
    terrace.ToTable("Terrace", "setup");

So the extractor recovered **1 declared mapping and guessed 123**, on a repository that states every
one of them outright. Every one of those 123 inferred `maps_to` edges was a name-matching guess
standing where a declaration already existed. The same reader also emitted the entity name as
written in source (`Order`) where every other assertion uses the display string (`Shop.Order`) — so
even its successes were edges whose subject matched no node.

Resolved semantically now: ask the model for the RECEIVER's type. One rule answers every style —
chained, local-variable, lambda-configuration, `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` — because in all of them
the receiver is an `EntityTypeBuilder<TEntity>`, and the symbol's display string is the name the rest
of the extractor emits. **Verified joins 1 → 64, inferred 123 → 73, `declares_table` facts 63.**

Generated files are skipped, on correctness grounds before performance ones: EF writes a model
snapshot per migration, each calling `ToTable` for every entity *as it stood then*, so reading them
asserts a table renamed three migrations ago as current fact wearing the same Verified badge. 63 of
the 66 files were these. `fluent-scan` fell 1,418ms → 60ms warm as a side effect, not as the goal.
The skip is disclosed with a count, because skipped is not absent.

DC-032 registered: **a reader recognises one spelling of a pattern and reports the rest as absent.**
The signature is a ratio nobody looks at — precise hits against fallback hits on real input — and it
survives because the fallback is doing its job, so the surface looks populated and coverage stays
green. The control was observed failing with the skip disabled.

**Module ids were colliding, certainly rather than theoretically.** Both module-shaped extractors
named a module by its path relative to its OWN SCOPE, and a scope is one directory. Every Python
package has an `__init__.py`, so a repository with five packages produced five scopes each declaring
a module called `__init__` — one node in the graph carrying the merged edges of five unrelated files.
The same for `index.ts`, `main`, `setup`, `conftest`. Ids are now the repository-relative path:
unique by construction, readable, and the string a person would type to open the file.

That made cross-scope resolution possible, which was the actual next step. An import naming a sibling
package resolves to a file in a different scope, so it could never resolve from inside the one doing
the importing. `ExtractionRequest` now carries the workspace's module set, computed once per revision
from the FILESYSTEM — not from the store, because resolving against what has already been extracted
would make an edge depend on the order the scopes happened to run in, the trap the Python extractor
already avoids one level down. Null means "not supplied", which is not "there is nothing there": the
edge stays Inferred and the disclosure fires.

A test comment had encoded the defective rule approvingly — *"modules are named relative to it:
`models`, not `src/models`"* — which is DC-031's tell in its own words.

**The graph surface is now queryable, not just fetchable.** `GraphQuery` filters by kind, by scope,
and by whether to include nodes nothing declares. The filter runs BEFORE the cap and degree is
counted over what survives it: filtering afterwards would rank and trim the whole graph and only then
discard, so a caller asking for the domain model would receive the wrong 5,000 nodes trimmed to the
right kind, with nothing in the result saying so. Proven across the daemon as well as in process,
because every cross-boundary defect here so far has been right in process and wrong through the pipe.

**A next step I listed last turn was wrong and is withdrawn.** "The index still walks every scope" —
it does not. `ScopeFingerprints` already skips an unchanged scope and counts it as *reused* rather
than *indexed*, deliberately, so "28 of 28 indexed" cannot be a true sentence about a run that read
nothing. I asserted its absence without opening the file. The residual — incrementality BELOW the
scope, so a one-file edit does not re-walk 1,026 types — is real, but it conflicts with the
append-only per-scope snapshot model and is a design decision, not a tidy-up.

717 tests green (App 121, Core 596). Six gates clean. Zero design-owned files.

title: Two more perf hypotheses died; routes, generated types, and a gate for every id allocator
summary:
Two more performance hypotheses died, and the second death is the useful one.

Splitting `depends_on`: **`SymbolEqualityComparer` dedupe is 3ms of 600ms — 0.5%** across 13,906 raw
symbols. Gather is 597ms. So the cost of `depends_on` IS the semantic work — `GetMembers()` binding
every member signature — and it cannot be made cheaper, only avoided. Two turns, two suspects
(`ToDisplayString` at 3.9%, then the comparer at 0.5%), both wrong, both named before being believed.
The measurement is now fine-grained enough that the next guess has nowhere to hide.

**Generated types are excluded from the whole extractor**, not just the fluent scan — a type is
dropped only when EVERY file declaring it is auto-generated, so a partial class with a hand-written
half (a WPF window, an EF migration people edit) is kept. Disclosed with a count.

**And the estimate that motivated it was wrong.** I predicted ~600 excluded types on TheTerrace. The
real number is **1**. EF marks only the snapshot half (`*.Designer.cs`) as generated; the migration
half starts with a plain `using System;`, so each migration type has a hand-written declaration and
is correctly kept. The rule is right and its effect here is small — recorded that way rather than
quietly dropped, because "I expected 600 and got 1" is the part worth knowing.

**Routes are answerable now.** `GraphPaths` returns how one node reaches another: shortest routes
only, directed (walking an edge backwards would answer "these are related" while looking like "a
change here reaches there"), with the route's status taken from its WEAKEST edge so one inferred link
cannot launder itself into a verified chain. A missing endpoint returns a reason, not an empty list
that reads as "unconnected". Proven across the daemon pipe as well as in process — a path is the one
result shaped as a list of lists, so it is the one most likely to arrive flattened.

**The id-allocator gap is closed, and closing it found two more allocators.**
`tools/verify-id-allocators.py` asks the generalising question behind DC-013 — *what else here is
numbered by reading the highest and adding one?* — as a check rather than a note. It guards five
families in one place (adding one is a line, not a script) and reports any UNDECLARED sequence, so
the next allocator is guarded on the day it is invented. Observed failing on both shapes before it
was believed.

On its first run it found `adr-` (16 decisions, allocated by FILENAME — a kind the first draft could
not even express) and, on inspection, `INV-`, which was below the threshold at two entries and was
declared anyway.

Two first-draft errors are recorded in DC-013 because they are the interesting part. It reported
eighteen holes in the audit log as failures — but a hole is the merge protocol working: a contested
id is resolved by re-issuing the loser, leaving the number unused. Verified with `git log -S`: none
of the missing ids has ever existed, so nothing was lost. **A control that flags the fix as the
defect is how a control teaches people to ignore it**, so contiguity is opt-in per family now. It
also first read ADR ids out of `architecture.md`, which only cites them — an allocator is where an id
is CREATED, never where it is mentioned.

**Electing a single allocator between sessions was considered and rejected** (the user asked). The
sessions work in separate worktrees on purpose and an election needs a rendezvous they do not have:
a session an hour into its work has not fetched, so "ask the allocator" is stale or a blocking round
trip through `main`, and it would make one session wait on another to record a lesson. The class is
not "the wrong allocator won", it is "a shared sequence with two writers".

**Sub-scope incrementality is written up, not built.** `docs/notes/note-20260830-sub-scope-
incrementality.md` states four options with what each costs, recommends one (keep the atomic
generation, skip the walk for unchanged types) and explicitly does not take it: the per-scope and
per-parse layers already exist, and nobody has measured whether edit-to-graph latency is a 1.2s
on-demand cost or a per-keystroke one. Instrumenting that is cheaper than any of the four options and
should come first. The decision changes the store's contract, so it is the user's call.

A build gap worth naming: the spike project is not in `AiDe.sln`, so last turn's solution build never
compiled it and the first measurement this turn silently ran a **stale binary**. Caught because the
new timing fields did not appear in the output.

730 tests green (App 123, Core 607). Six gates clean, one of them new. Zero design-owned files.

title: Refresh cost measured, no project uncompiled, DC-033 swept, routes on a surface
summary:
**The measurement the sub-scope decision was blocked on now exists.** A refresh had a span but its
STATUS carried no duration, so the only thing a caller could read was how many assertions came back.
`ScopeRefreshStatus` now carries `QueuedMilliseconds` and `DurationMilliseconds` — kept separate
because waiting is a concurrency problem and running is a cost problem, and one number hides which
one a user is feeling. `RefreshMetrics` adds p50/p95/max over a bounded window plus first/last
observed, exposed over IPC as `refresh.metrics` with no request body and no failure mode: an operator
asking what re-indexing costs should never be told it depends on what they enable first.

Deliberately **no rate is computed**. "Refreshes per hour" from two samples is a number with no error
bar that gets quoted as if it had one; the raw facts let a reader compute it when there is enough of
it to mean something and notice when there is not. Failed refreshes are timed too — a run that takes
twenty seconds and then throws is the one an operator most wants to see, and excluding failures is
how a percentile ends up describing only the easy cases. With nothing measured everything reports
zero and null rather than an interpolation of nothing.

**No tracked project escapes compilation now.** `spikes/joins-on-a-real-repo` — the harness behind
nearly every performance and join number in this log — is not in `AiDe.sln`, so a change to
`GraphAsync` broke it while the solution build stayed green, and the next measurement silently ran a
STALE BINARY. Caught only because an expected timing field did not appear. Had the change not added a
field, the numbers would have looked fine and been wrong. That is DC-023 with a twist: the gate was
not stale, it was NARROW.

`tools/verify-project-coverage.py` builds every tracked project the solution does not contain. A
gate rather than solution membership, because `AiDe.sln` answers "what ships" and these are evidence
artifacts. **The cost claim in its own header was wrong and is corrected in place:** it was written
expecting to belong in the slow at-readiness ring and measures **16 seconds for 19 projects**, which
puts it on every push. It prints its wall time on every run so that stays a measured decision.
Observed failing against a deliberately broken spike.

**DC-033 swept, and it found a second instance.** The class says its signature is a ratio on real
input, so the sweep measured. `TypeScriptExtractor` knew `class|interface|type|enum|function|const`
and did not know `async`, the generator star, `namespace`, `let` or `var`. TheTerrace declares 124
`export interface`, 26 `export type`, 16 `export const` and **4 `export namespace`** — four
declarations reported as absent rather than unread. `PythonExtractor` is clean; the Bicep and schema
readers are narrow by *declared* ceiling and disclose it.

The important half is not the wider pattern, which will be wrong again for the next spelling. **The
reader now counts its own misses and discloses them** — `typescript-exports-not-recognised (N)` — so
the next unanticipated form announces itself on the scope. Re-exports are excluded deliberately:
counting them gives a miss rate that never reaches zero and therefore says nothing.

**Routes reach a surface.** `CanvasGraphViewModel.RouteAsync(from, to)` returns the **same
`CanvasGraph`** the canvas already binds, because a route IS a subgraph and giving it its own shape
would mean a second renderer and a second place for the two sessions to disagree about what a node
looks like. Endpoints arrive with `IsRoot = true`; the caption names the count, the shortest length
and **the weakest link**, because a route drawn without that looks like a fact about the code when
one inferred edge makes the whole claim inferred. Every empty case says which one it is, and the
projection's own reason survives to the caption — "not in this graph" and "no route within 8 edges"
send a user to different places.

**The `GraphQuery` filter question is put to the design session as a decision, not a request.** All
three filters are on the wire and proven across the daemon; which of them belong in the UI, and as
what control, is an information-architecture call this session does not own. §4a states the three
with what each is worth, recommends a **preset** over toggles (three named views are one decision a
user makes once; three toggles are a combinatorial space they must reason about) and says plainly
that this is a guess about users. What Core commits to either way is the tested property: the filter
runs before the cap and degree is computed over what survives it.

765 tests green (App 131, Core 634). Seven gates clean, one of them new.
Zero design-owned files.

title: INV-0003: the graph could not fit through the pipe, and the default should never have asked
summary:
The graph pane has been broken on TheTerrace since the whole-graph change, and it is my defect. The
design session investigated it (INV-0003), verified the cause and handed it to Core.

MEASURED: the whole-graph response is 1,522,284 bytes against a 1,048,576-byte IPC frame. It could
never have been delivered. `IpcFraming.WriteAsync` threw, the serve loop caught `IOException` and
`OperationCanceledException` but not that, the exception escaped, the connection closed with no
reply — so "the answer is too big to send" reached the user as "the daemon closed the connection
without responding", which sends them to look at the daemon.

Two fixes, both Core's:

**The transport no longer closes silently.** `IpcServer.Respond` checks the encoded size BEFORE
writing and returns a new `ipc.payload_too_large` carrying the actual and permitted byte counts.
Checked before rather than caught after on purpose: a partially written frame leaves the peer reading
a length prefix whose body never arrives, which is a hang rather than an error. The writer's own throw
is correct and stays.

**The default view is bounded by construction.** No focus now asks for 1,500 declared nodes ranked by
degree rather than the whole graph — 533,495 bytes, fits, 618 omitted and named in the caption.

The transport failure exposed the larger error, and the design session is right about it: the fix for
DC-031 over-corrected. The graph pane rendering two nodes of two thousand was a real defect; loading
EVERYTHING overshot the spec that was being restored — `knowledge-exploration.md` US-K2 already said
the whole graph is never rendered at once. The answer to "one arbitrary alphabetical node" was a
bounded overview of MEANINGFUL nodes. DC-031 and DC-035 are the same axis overshot in opposite
directions, and a fix for one lands on the other unless the spec is re-read when the new default is
chosen. That is recorded on DC-035 as mine.

Bounding by size and bounding by meaning turned out to be the same change: measured, the six
most-connected nodes of a real repository were `string`, `int`, `Task<T>`, `DateTimeOffset`,
`IReadOnlyList<T>` and `Guid`, so a first view centred on the BCL was unreadable as well as
undeliverable.

DC-035 moves from `uncontrolled` to `partially-controlled`. Core's half is landed and tested,
including the byte measurements pinned as an assertion so that raising the frame cap without
revisiting the default fails there first. **Design's half is open and named:** the aggregated /
level-of-detail overview for a graph too large to show node-by-node, and the "narrow your focus"
state. Until that exists a repository whose declared code exceeds the cap gets a truthful truncation
rather than a designed overview.

775 tests green (App 131, Core 639). Seven gates clean. Zero design-owned files.

title: Every response is bounded by bytes, and the incrementality question answered by a grep
summary:
The graph was found by a user opening a repository, not by us, so every other read operation was
measured at its own ceiling against the 1 MiB frame. **Two more were one repository away from
INV-0003, and a third could never have succeeded.**

| operation | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| evidence (2,000/page) | 1,004,397 B — **95.8% of the frame** | 659,164 B, 1,310 rows, cursor continues |
| graph (5,000-node ceiling) | 1,522,915 B — **overflows** | 474,437 B, shrunk to fit, `Omitted` reports |
| find (20,000 ceiling) | 461,750 B returned while **reporting a 64 KiB cap** | byte-bounded, `ByteCapped` set |

The class behind all three: **every ceiling in the read surface counts ITEMS and the transport limit
is in BYTES**, and every item's size comes from repository content. A count-only cap admits an
unbounded payload. `Evidence`'s own documentation claimed a page "can cross a pipe without breaching
the result-byte cap" — it was fifteen times over that cap. `Find` declared `MaxBytes: 65,536` beside
461,750 bytes of results, a control that could not fire (DC-016).

Truncating an evidence page is **lossless**, which is why the bound belongs in the projection: the
cursor continues from the last row actually returned, so it costs a round trip and never a row. A
test pages a corpus to exhaustion and asserts every assertion comes back exactly once. Every response
keeps at least one item — a caller that receives nothing because its first row is enormous can never
make progress.

The byte guard uses a **measured** constant, not a guessed one: 2,000 assertions whose fields total
238,002 bytes serialise to 1,004,397, so JSON scaffolding is **383 bytes per row**. Rounded up,
because a guard that under-counts is a guard that lets the frame overflow.

**The sub-scope-incrementality decision is resolved, and not by the instrument built for it.** The
note said the answer depended on how often edit-to-graph happens, and `RefreshMetrics` was built to
measure that. One grep answered it instead: **there is no `FileSystemWatcher` anywhere in `src/`**.
Indexing runs only from explicit commands, so the cost is paid deliberately by a user pressing a
button. Breaking the per-scope snapshot's atomicity to shorten a deliberate 1.2s action is a poor
trade, so none of options A–D is built. The note stays, status `resolved`, naming the trigger that
would change it: **re-index on save**, which converts a bounded cost into a per-edit one.

Worth recording because it nearly went the other way. Three hypotheses in this area have now been
wrong — `ToDisplayString` (3.9%), `SymbolEqualityComparer` (0.5%), "the index still walks every
scope" (it does not). This would have been the fourth: collecting a distribution and reasoning
carefully about a number that answered a question nobody was asking.

**My own new gate cried wolf and is fixed.** `verify-id-allocators` reported an undeclared family
called `nDC-` — it was matching the `n` of a JSON-escaped newline before a *mentioned* `DC-` id in a
log summary. A mention is not an allocation, which is the same distinction the first draft got wrong
when it read ADR ids out of `architecture.md`. Fixed with a lookbehind, and the narrative files are
excluded from the candidate scan: a record of a mention must never nominate an allocator. This is the
second time this script has flagged correct behaviour as a defect; a control that does that twice is
one people switch off.

790 tests green (App 131, Core 645). Seven gates clean. Zero design-owned files.

title: The workspace as groups: the aggregated overview, and a reflective frame-fit gate
summary:
**The aggregated overview closes Core's half of DC-035.** The bounded default fixed the transport
failure by drawing 1,500 of 2,118 declared nodes and saying so — honest, and still a truncation. A
user opening a repository wants its SHAPE, and 1,500 dots is not a shape.

`GraphOverview` returns the workspace as GROUPS, grouped by the ids' own hierarchy — a C# symbol is
`TheTerrace.Features.Competitions.Season`, a module is `src/app/models`, so the first `Depth`
segments name what a developer would call "where that lives", and Depth is the zoom control.

MEASURED on TheTerrace at depth 3: `Features.Fixtures` 117, `Features.Teams` 117, `Features.Matches`
107, `Infrastructure.Data` 70, `Features.Identity` 47, `Features.Competitions` 44 — the actual shape
of that repository, in **55,758 bytes** against 533,484 for the node graph.

**No community-detection algorithm, deliberately.** Its output is unstable under small changes to the
graph, so the same repository would regroup between two indexes and the picture would move for
reasons the user cannot see. Prefix grouping is stable by construction.

Each group carries `NodeCount` — a dot standing for 240 types is only honest while the 240 is on it,
which is the whole difference between an overview and a smaller lie. Each link carries `Weight` for
thickness and the **weakest** status of the edges it bundles, because drawing a bundle as Verified
because most of its members were would launder guesses into facts at a grain where the user can no
longer see the members. Edges inside a group are counted, not drawn.

**My own first default was the failure the overview exists to prevent.** `MaxClusters` shipped at 200,
and TheTerrace has 689 groups at depth 3 — returning 200 of them is a hairball at a coarser grain,
which my own doc comment named as the thing to avoid. Measured and lowered to 60.

**The frame-fit control is reflective, because hand-auditing found the last three and would not find
the next.** `EveryOperationFitsTheFrameTests` derives the operation list from `IWorkspaceQueries`
itself and fails when a method is added with no size check — observed failing with an entry removed,
naming the method. Writing the list by hand would restate the product's own list (DC-021) and go
stale in exactly the case that matters.

**The write side was audited and needs nothing.** An `IndexSummary` for 28 scopes is **1,724 bytes** —
three orders of magnitude below the frame. Recorded rather than guarded: a control whose failure
nobody can name is one to drop.

**Degree on the wire was already done, by the other session.** They shipped force-directed layout with
degree-sized dots (DC-036), so that next step was stale when I wrote it. What layout still could not
do is cluster, which is what the overview provides. `GraphOverview.GroupFor` is public now so the
canvas groups detail nodes the SAME way the overview does — two definitions of one grouping is
DC-022's shape, and the divergence would render a node in the wrong cluster and look like a layout
bug.

**A shared test double replaces four hand-written stubs.** Every method added to `IWorkspaceQueries`
has broken the same four stubs across two projects — four rounds of identical churn, which is a
measured recurrence rather than a predicted one. `FakeWorkspaceQueries` throws rather than returning
empty: a stub that quietly answers a question the test did not intend to ask turns a wrong call site
into a passing test.

791 tests green (App 132, Core 659). Seven gates clean. Zero design-owned files.

title: Drill-down closes the overview loop, and a third repository found a defect in my own control
summary:
**Drill-down closes the loop the overview opened.** `GraphQuery.GroupId` returns the nodes inside one
cluster, and the depth is read back out of the group id rather than passed alongside it — a separate
depth parameter would let a caller ask for `TheTerrace.Features` at depth 3 and receive nothing, with
no error and no way to tell that from an empty group.

The property that makes the overview trustworthy is asserted, not assumed: **every cluster's
`NodeCount` equals what drilling into it returns**, and every cluster's `InternalEdges` equals what
drilling in draws. For every group, not a sampled one — the interesting failure is the group whose
naming rule differs, and that is never the group a test author picks by hand. Both paths compute
membership from one definition (`GraphOverview.GroupFor`), which is why the round trip holds.

**Proven across the pipe.** The overview is nested — clusters and weighted links — so it is the
response most likely to arrive with an inner list flattened or a count defaulted to zero, and a
cluster's count is a claim a user can check. The daemon test now drills from the largest cluster back
to its nodes and asserts the counts agree.

**Three repositories now, not one — and the third one found a defect in my own control.** Every
measurement in this project had come from TheTerrace. Running BioHacker (32 scopes, no `DbContext` at
all, so 0 joins is correct rather than a failure) and meridian-finance-planner (31 scopes, 9,165
assertions, 165 TypeScript files) confirmed every operation fits the frame on all three.

BioHacker reported `typescript-exports-not-recognised (1)` — the DC-033 control firing on the first
new repository it saw, which is what it is for. But the miss was **mine**: `export default
defineConfig({…})` and `export default test;` declare nothing new, and the miss-counter's own doc
comment said `export default someExpression` was excluded while the pattern never excluded it.
`export default` is ubiquitous, so the disclosure would have fired on nearly every real TypeScript
codebase and become noise. Fixed; the 165-file repository now reports zero.

**The shape is worth naming because it is the third instance this session.** The exclusion was written
in the comment before it was implemented — exactly like the evidence page documenting a byte cap it
did not apply, and `find` reporting a `MaxBytes` it never enforced. **A claim in prose that the code
does not make true.** When a comment states a bound, the next question is which line applies it.

And the meta-lesson, recorded on DC-033: **a control's false-positive rate is only observable on input
it was not written against.** Validating on one repository validates against one repository.

**The shared test double now covers both projects.** `FakeWorkspaceQueries` moved to `tests/Shared`
under a neutral namespace and is linked into both test csproj files — linked source rather than a new
assembly, because a project for forty lines is more machinery than the churn it removes. The two
App-project stubs that hand-implemented the whole seam now override only what they answer.

800 tests green (App 132, Core 668). Seven gates clean. Zero design-owned files.

title: Knowledge exploration becomes a full-window Explorer mode (dual-pane graph+reader), not a dock pane
prompt: reconsider the graph view as a full-window dual-pane surface entered from a rail icon
summary: Specified a distinct 'primary view mode' (Workbench | Explorer): a rail icon slides the exploration open body-wide with graph+search | reader, reusing the existing reader (US-K3) and node-walk (US-K4). Additive and toggleable; docked graph pane can remain during rollout.
rationale: On a single monitor the docked graph pane competes with reading a node's contents; a dedicated full-window dual-pane mode is the requested remedy and matches the VS Code/JetBrains/Obsidian idiom.

title: A comment that states a bound the code does not apply, and raw SQL schemas read
summary:
**The sweep found the class was live in the tree, and the class now has a control.**

Three instances this session were the same shape — a comment states a bound the code does not apply.
The sweep found a fourth still standing: `MaxEvidencePageCeiling` documented as "sized so a page
stays comfortably inside `MaxResultBytes`" when 2,000 assertions serialise to **1,004,397 bytes**,
fifteen times that constant. Corrected to name the mechanism that actually bounds it.

`tools/verify-bounds-are-enforced.py` requires every constant whose NAME claims a limit to appear in
a comparison, a clamp or a take — searched over code with comments stripped, so prose cannot count as
proof. On its first run it found `WholeGraphNodeCap`: declared last turn as a "retained name",
documented as a ceiling, **zero usages**. Deleted. One false positive (`OverviewNodeCap`, applied
indirectly through `GraphQuery.MaxNodes`) became a justified exemption rather than a weaker rule,
because "it is passed somewhere" is exactly what made `find` look safe.

**The control says what it cannot do.** It checks a bound is APPLIED, not that a sentence describing
it is TRUE — the TypeScript instance, a regex differing from its comment, is invisible to it. Half
the class is mechanised; claiming otherwise would be this class applied to its own control.

**Measurement is repeatable now.** `tools/measure-repositories.py` runs the harness over three
codebases chosen for contrast and prints them side by side. It exists because every number in this
project came from one repository until a second was tried by hand, and the third exposed a defect in
a control that looked correct against the first.

**The overview's default depth was the useless one, and three repositories showed it:**

    TheTerrace                d1:  74 groups,  1 link    d2: 200,  6    d3: 200, 263
